spirits.name: Adze
spirits.shortDescription: A tiny night-light looking for a gentler glow.
spirits.folklore: In Ewe traditions, adze is associated with harmful spirit power and witchcraft; some accounts describe a firefly form. These meanings belong to particular communities and tellers, rather than to all West African folklore. Our glowing toy is a friendly festival reinterpretation, not a depiction of a real person accused of witchcraft.
spirits.wish: Light a path without frightening anyone.

story.title: Too bright tonight
story.text: The little adze flashed beside a dark garden path. Every time a visitor approached, the light flared so brightly that nobody stopped to say hello.

story.title: A softer sparkle
story.text: Your candy gift became a tiny dewdrop lantern. The adze tucked the bright glow inside and watched it turn warm and soft.

story.title: Follow the little light
story.text: Soon a line of friends followed the gentle sparkle home. The adze no longer needed to outshine the stars; one welcoming light was enough.

sources.title: Eric Montgomery, Ewe spirit traditions, eTropic

spirits.name: Asanbosam
spirits.shortDescription: A treetop visitor with a very careful embrace.
spirits.folklore: Asanbosam is a forest being in Akan traditions, especially accounts associated with present-day Ghana. Hook-like feet and a threatening presence appear in familiar descriptions, while names and features vary between tellings. This little collectible softens those forms into rounded shapes; its leafy scarf and helpful personality are original additions.
spirits.wish: Make a resting place that everyone can share.

story.title: An empty branch
story.text: Asanbosam had found the best branch in the forest, but the little hooked feet kept catching the picnic blanket. There was nowhere comfortable for a guest.

story.title: A careful knot
story.text: Your candy gift became a bundle of soft ribbons. Working slowly, the forest visitor tied the blanket into a hammock and tucked each hook safely away.

story.title: A place beside me
story.text: By moonrise, the hammock held a cushion for every friend. Asanbosam waved from the leafy shade, delighted that the best view could finally be shared.

sources.title: Sasabonsam: Akan folklore and reference bibliography

spirits.name: Tokoloshe
spirits.shortDescription: A shaggy little visitor listening beside the reeds.
spirits.folklore: Tokoloshe, also spelled tikoloshe, appears in several Southern African language traditions, including isiZulu and isiXhosa. Descriptions often present a small hairy being associated with water, mischief or harm. Accounts differ across communities. The smooth pebble and peaceful riverside wish belong to this game, not to a traditional protective practice.
spirits.wish: Hear a friendly answer across the water.

story.title: Only an echo
story.text: Beside a pool, the tokoloshe called a small hello. The reeds rustled back, but the little visitor could not tell whether anyone had heard.

story.title: Circles on the water
story.text: Your candy gift made the blue pebble shimmer. A gentle tap sent bright circles across the pool, carrying the greeting toward the other bank.

story.title: Hello from the reeds
story.text: Another circle came drifting back. Friends were waiting beside the reeds, and the tokoloshe settled down to trade quiet greetings until the moon rose.

sources.title: Dictionary of South African English: tokoloshe

spirits.name: Kalanoro
spirits.shortDescription: A small forest visitor with a leaf-filled satchel.
spirits.folklore: Kalanoro are nature spirits in Malagasy traditions. Ethnographic accounts from northern Madagascar describe small, long-haired beings and their relationships with certain specialists and local places. These are living, varied traditions, not a single island-wide fairy story. Our leaf satchel and garden adventure are an original gentle interpretation.
spirits.wish: Find a sheltered home for a wandering seed.

story.title: The last seed
story.text: The kalanoro carried one seed in a leaf satchel. Every clearing seemed too windy, and every hollow too dark for the small green life inside.

story.title: A pocket of warmth
story.text: Your candy gift became a warm glimmer under a broad leaf. The kalanoro discovered a patch of soft soil where the wind could not reach.

story.title: Tomorrow in a leaf
story.text: A tiny shoot greeted the morning. The kalanoro curled up beside it, knowing the long search had ended in a place where something new could grow.

sources.title: Lesley A. Sharp, The Possessed and the Dispossessed, chapter 5

spirits.name: Ghul
spirits.shortDescription: A lantern-bearing wanderer learning the way home.
spirits.folklore: The ghul belongs to Arabic supernatural storytelling and is often associated with deserted places, danger and changing shape. Later literary and popular versions differ, and the English word ghoul does not capture every earlier meaning. This hooded, lantern-bearing visitor is an original gentle design rather than a traditional fixed appearance.
spirits.wish: Mark a path that leads travelers safely home.

story.title: A turn too many
story.text: The little ghul knew every winding path, yet tonight even the familiar dunes looked different. A lantern swung quietly beside an empty crossroads.

story.title: Small lights ahead
story.text: Your candy gift lit a row of warm markers. The ghul followed them one by one, pausing to set each crooked marker straight.

story.title: A welcome at the end
story.text: The last marker pointed to a gathering of friends. Now the ghul had a route worth remembering, and a lantern ready for the next traveler.

spirits.name: Ifrit
spirits.shortDescription: A bright little ember with a warmhearted wish.
spirits.folklore: Ifrit names a formidable supernatural being in Arabic and Islamic traditions and appears in literary tales such as the Arabian Nights. Its uses and character vary across texts and communities; it is not simply a universal fire monster. The ember body, lantern and friendly festival personality here are original visual choices.
spirits.wish: Keep one little lantern warm all night.

story.title: An impatient flame
story.text: The ifrit could make a grand burst of light, but the little lantern needed a steady glow. Each excited flicker made its flame wobble.

story.title: A patient spark
story.text: Your candy gift became a copper cradle for the ember. The ifrit took a slow breath and watched the light settle into a gentle rhythm.

story.title: Still shining
story.text: When morning reached the windows, the lantern was still warm. The ifrit smiled: a small kindness kept glowing longer than the biggest flash.

spirits.name: Marid
spirits.shortDescription: A grand swirling visitor with a very small treasure.
spirits.folklore: Marid is a term for a powerful or rebellious supernatural being in Arabic traditions. In some Arabian Nights translations, marid and ifrit can describe the same being rather than separate species. Our teal swirling form and pearl-like bead distinguish this festival character visually; they do not claim that all marids are water spirits.
spirits.wish: Carry a tiny treasure without losing it.

story.title: Too much breeze
story.text: The marid arrived in a wonderful whirl, and the little bead rolled straight out of reach. Such a small treasure was surprisingly difficult to carry.

story.title: A quieter current
story.text: Your candy gift made a soft pouch of cloud. The marid slowed the swirling breeze and nestled the bead carefully inside.

story.title: Something to cherish
story.text: At the party, the marid opened the pouch to show the friends. The treasure had arrived safely, carried by the gentlest swirl in the sky.

sources.title: Edward William Lane, The Thousand and One Nights, The Fisherman

spirits.name: Nasnas
spirits.shortDescription: One springy foot and a whole lot of curiosity.
spirits.folklore: The nasnas appears in Arabic marvel literature and later accounts of Arabian tales. A familiar description gives it one arm and one leg, with a remarkably agile hop. Versions and uses of the name differ. Our rounded, one-eyed felt creature is a non-graphic fantasy interpretation, not a comparison with human bodies or disability.
spirits.wish: Find a rhythm that friends can follow.

story.title: A rhythm of one
story.text: The nasnas hopped toward the music, but every tune seemed to hurry past. The little scarf bobbed while one foot tried to keep the beat.

story.title: A kinder tempo
story.text: Your candy gift became a bright tinkling note. The nasnas tried a slower rhythm, and the friends began tapping along.

story.title: Everyone in step
story.text: Soon the whole path rang with different footsteps. The nasnas led the parade at a happy pace, with room in the music for every kind of dancer.

spirits.name: Div
spirits.shortDescription: A little giant building something thoughtful.
spirits.folklore: Divs are powerful beings in Persian epic and folktale, including the Shahnameh. They can appear as adversaries, sorcerers or, in some narratives, helpers and builders. Their forms and actions vary widely. This small indigo toy keeps an ogre-like silhouette while giving it a new, friendly building project.
spirits.wish: Build a doorstep small enough for a friend.

story.title: A giant-sized problem
story.text: The div built a splendid doorway, then noticed the doorstep was much too tall. The smallest friend could see the welcome light but could not reach it.

story.title: One stone at a time
story.text: Your candy gift showed where to place the little stones. The div stacked them carefully into a gentle stair, checking each step with a fingertip.

story.title: Come right in
story.text: Every friend could now reach the door. The div sat beside the tiny staircase, proud that the best building was one that made visitors feel welcome.

spirits.name: Pari
spirits.shortDescription: A petal-winged visitor tending one late blossom.
spirits.folklore: Pari has a long history in Iranian traditions, with meanings that changed across periods and texts. Later Persian stories often describe beautiful fairy-like beings, while earlier related terms can have darker associations. Our petal wings and flower-carrying design draw on the later fairy-like image without treating every tradition as identical.
spirits.wish: Help one late flower open before the festival.

story.title: Still a little bud
story.text: The pari had brought a flower for the festival, but its petals stayed folded. Around it, every lantern was already shining.

story.title: A patient glow
story.text: Your candy gift warmed the air around the bud. The pari waited quietly, turning it toward the soft light instead of pulling at its petals.

story.title: Right on time
story.text: The flower opened as the first friend arrived. The pari smiled behind the bright petals; some welcomes simply needed a little more time.

spirits.name: Shahmaran
spirits.shortDescription: A gentle queen guarding a quiet garden.
spirits.folklore: Shahmaran is a serpent queen in stories shared across Anatolian, Kurdish and neighboring traditions. Regional versions, including accounts associated with Tarsus, connect her with hidden places, knowledge, trust and betrayal. This crowned figure retains a human upper body and serpentine lower body; the welcoming garden ending is newly written for this festival.
spirits.wish: Open a garden where every guest feels safe.

story.title: Beyond the gate
story.text: Shahmaran tended a quiet garden whose gate had stayed closed for years. A golden flower leaned toward the sound of footsteps outside.

story.title: A sign of welcome
story.text: Your candy gift lit a small path through the leaves. Shahmaran placed the flower beside the gate and gently opened it.

story.title: Trust in bloom
story.text: Friends entered softly and left every blossom growing. Curled beside the path, Shahmaran watched the garden become a place of shared care.

sources.title: Türkiye Culture Portal: Shahmaran of Tarsus

spirits.name: Karakoncolos
spirits.shortDescription: A shaggy winter caller with softly ringing bells.
spirits.folklore: Karakoncolos belongs to winter folklore in Türkiye and neighboring regions, with local names and descriptions. Turkish cultural records describe shaggy figures, bells and sticks among its varied features. Our little visitor keeps that wintry silhouette while replacing frightening encounters with an original story about a gentle bell.
spirits.wish: Ring a welcome without waking the whole valley.

story.title: A noisy arrival
story.text: The karakoncolos came down the snowy path with bells ringing everywhere. Even the sleepy lantern keeper jumped at the sound.

story.title: Wrapped in warmth
story.text: Your candy gift became a soft ribbon around the largest bell. The winter visitor tried again, listening to the quiet chime between footsteps.

story.title: A bell at the door
story.text: This time the door opened with a smile. The karakoncolos shook the snow from the shaggy coat and settled beside friends in the warm light.

spirits.name: Zheztyrnak
spirits.shortDescription: Copper fingers catching the last evening light.
spirits.folklore: Zheztyrnak, also written Jeztyrnaq, is a dangerous figure with copper or brass claws in Kazakh folklore. Stories often place the encounter in wild country, where a traveler must recognize a threat. Our rounded copper fingers and gentle craft activity are deliberate festival inventions, not a claim that the traditional figure was harmless.
spirits.wish: Make a lantern without snagging its paper.

story.title: Paper and copper
story.text: Zheztyrnak wanted to make a lantern, but every sheet caught on the long copper fingers. The little pile of paper grew while the sky grew dark.

story.title: A softer touch
story.text: Your candy gift became a pair of smooth wooden guides. With slow, careful movements, the mountain visitor folded one bright sheet around them.

story.title: Light in the hands
story.text: The finished lantern shone against the copper fingers. Zheztyrnak held it gently, ready to join the other lights along the mountain path.

spirits.name: Albasty
spirits.shortDescription: A long-haired visitor beside a moonlit stream.
spirits.folklore: Albasty appears in several Central Asian and other Turkic traditions, including Kazakh accounts. Stories often associate the figure with water, danger and fears around childbirth, but descriptions vary. This long-haired, reed-carrying collectible is an original gentle adaptation; its story does not present folklore as a medical explanation.
spirits.wish: Untangle a reed song caught in the wind.

story.title: A tangled tune
story.text: The albasty listened beside the stream, where a knot of reeds had fallen silent. Even the evening breeze could not coax a song from them.

story.title: One strand at a time
story.text: Your candy gift made each bent stem glimmer. The visitor carefully loosened the bundle and set the reeds apart along the bank.

story.title: Music on the water
story.text: The next breeze carried a soft tune across the stream. The albasty rested beside the reeds, long hair stirring gently with the music.

sources.title: Inzhuna Karazhanova, Monstrous femininity in Kazakh folklore

spirits.name: Zhalmauyz Kempir
spirits.shortDescription: An old story visitor saving a seat for company.
spirits.folklore: Zhalmauyz Kempir is an old ogress figure in Kazakh fairy tales, with related figures in neighboring Turkic traditions. Her role is not identical in every tale: scholarship discusses both threatening and more ambiguous appearances. Our single-faced elder, teacup and hospitable ending are original festival choices rather than a summary of every traditional version.
spirits.wish: Share the last warm cup with a visitor.

story.title: An extra cup
story.text: Zhalmauyz Kempir set out a cup beside the fire. The tea was warm, the chair was empty, and every sound outside seemed to hurry past the door.

story.title: A light in the window
story.text: Your candy gift became a little window lantern. Its glow showed travelers that someone was waiting with a seat and a story.

story.title: Stay for a tale
story.text: At last a friend knocked. The old visitor poured the tea and began a story so curious that nobody noticed the night turning toward morning.

sources.title: Inzhuna Karazhanova, Monstrous femininity in Kazakh folklore

spirits.name: Zhalgyz Koz
spirits.shortDescription: One big eye noticing the smallest things.
spirits.folklore: The one-eyed giant, Zhalgyz kozdi dau, appears in Kazakh fairy-tale scholarship and collections. Such giants belong to narratives of encounters, danger and ingenuity, rather than to a documented animal species. This miniature woolly visitor has one central eye and a small stone prop; its helpful search is an original festival story.
spirits.wish: Find the little stone that completes a path.

story.title: A gap in the path
story.text: The little giant noticed a missing stone where visitors crossed the stream. A large stride could pass it easily, but smaller footsteps needed help.

story.title: Looking closely
story.text: Your candy gift lit the pebbles along the bank. With one patient eye, the giant searched until a smooth stone of just the right shape appeared.

story.title: Every step matters
story.text: The stone fitted perfectly. The giant waited beside the crossing, happy to see even the smallest friend reach the other side with dry feet.

sources.title: Tursunova et al., study of Kazakh fairy tales
